Optical character recog-
nition has a long history,
and the problems it faces
on a screen are not the
problems it faces on a
page. A scanned docu-
ment arrives with paper
texture, skew, and bleed-
through from the reverse
side. A screen region ar-
rives clean, perfectly
axis aligned, and free of
noise, but it arrives at
whatever size the dis-
play happened to render
it.

That difference matters
more than it first ap-

than any amount of
clever thresholding.

Background polarity is
the other common trap.
A great deal of text on a
modern desktop is light
on a dark background,
which is the inverse of
every page the engine
was trained on. Modern
engines cope with this
better than they once
did, but making the in-
put uniform costs almost
nothing and removes a
variable from every
measurement taken
downstream.
